books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Henry Clay, resolutions offered in the Senate, January 29, 1850

stimulus.source_note: Henry Clay, resolutions offered in the Senate, January 29, 1850 (Congressional Globe, 31st Congress, 1st session). Public domain.
stimulus.text:
It being desirable, for the peace, concord, and harmony of the Union of these States, to settle and adjust amicably all existing questions of controversy between them arising out of the institution of slavery upon a fair, equitable and just basis: therefore,

1. Resolved, That California, with suitable boundaries, ought, upon her application to be admitted as one of the States of this Union, without the imposition by Congress of any restriction in respect to the exclusion or introduction of slavery within those boundaries.

2. Resolved, That as slavery does not exist by law, and is not likely to be introduced into any of the territory acquired by the United States from the republic of Mexico, it is inexpedient for Congress to provide by law either for its introduction into, or exclusion from, any part of the said territory; and that appropriate territorial governments ought to be established by Congress in all of the said territory, not assigned as the boundaries of the proposed State of California, without the adoption of any restriction or condition on the subject of slavery.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Clay's second resolution treats slavery in the Mexican Cession by arguing that Congress should

options.text: ban slavery in every territory taken from Mexico.
options.misconception: Banning slavery is what Clay refuses to do here; he calls providing for its exclusion inexpedient.

options.text: extend the Missouri Compromise line to the Pacific coast.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the Missouri Compromise line is not mentioned in these resolutions; Clay never proposes extending it westward.

options.text: let the Supreme Court decide whether slavery could enter the territories.
options.misconception: The resolutions give the courts no role; they ask Congress itself to organize territorial governments.

options.text: leave the question alone and organize territorial governments with no slavery restriction.

rationales.A: Banning slavery is what Clay refuses to do here; he calls providing for its exclusion inexpedient.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the Missouri Compromise line is not mentioned in these resolutions; Clay never proposes extending it westward.
rationales.C: The resolutions give the courts no role; they ask Congress itself to organize territorial governments.
rationales.D: The second resolution calls it “inexpedient for Congress to provide by law either for its introduction into, or exclusion from, any part of the said territory,” and asks for territorial governments “without the adoption of any restriction or condition on the subject of slavery.”
rationales.general:
1. Find the key word in the second resolution: “inexpedient,” meaning unwise to do.
2. Ask what Clay calls unwise: Congress providing by law either for slavery's introduction or for its exclusion.
3. Notice the result: territorial governments with no slavery condition at all, so Congress decides nothing.
Remember: when a lawmaker calls both choices unwise, he is choosing to decide nothing.
